name: Barbara Webb
role: Professor of Biorobotics, School of Informatics, University of Edinburgh
need: Circuit-generated reinforcement and competing memory timescales
title: An incentive circuit for memory dynamics in the mushroom body of Drosophila melanogaster
finding: The computational model combines a proposed dopamine-dependent plasticity rule with identified mushroom-body feedback motifs to reproduce acquisition, forgetting and memory assimilation. It tests neural-response and simulated behavioral patterns.
second: Insect Robotics research program
https://homepages.inf.ed.ac.uk/bwebb/
Current computational and physical models of insect perception, navigation and learning; methodology of measurement and simulation.
background: An AI PhD and psychology background underpin her use of computational and robotic insect models to test biological explanations. Her current profile explicitly lists fly learning and modeling methodology.
question: Which independent neural-response prediction would distinguish a missing feedback circuit from an incorrect local plasticity rule in a model that fails reversal?
test: Proposed: preregister competing circuit and local-rule explanations, preserve graph identity, and evaluate cue-specific dopamine/output responses and reversal under matched feedback controls. An anatomical mapping and primary physiological justification are prerequisites.
limit: The reduced incentive circuit is not a validated full FlyWire chess learner. Webb overlaps with already-contacted Nitabach and McCurdy on the same paper; this is additional modeling expertise, not an independent biological replication.
paragraph: Your eLife incentive-circuit model is close to the question I am struggling with: a learning rule may look reasonable on its own, yet fail because the feedback circuit around it is missing something. I noticed that your study checks both neural response patterns and behavior across different memory stages. Before changing my model after a failed reversal, which independent neural-response prediction would help distinguish an incorrect local rule from a missing feedback interaction?
subject: Student mentorship inquiry: testing the circuit behind failed memory reversal
body:
Dear Professor Webb,

I'm Ethan Ramli, a 16-year-old Singaporean grade 11 student in Jakarta. Chess and the public adult fly connectome led me to ask whether a model constrained by that wiring could learn useful decisions through experience and feedback.

Your eLife incentive-circuit model is close to the question I am struggling with: a learning rule may look reasonable on its own, yet fail because the feedback circuit around it is missing something. I noticed that your study checks both neural response patterns and behavior across different memory stages. Before changing my model after a failed reversal, which independent neural-response prediction would help distinguish an incorrect local rule from a missing feedback interaction?

In six runs of a simple association experiment, the prototype preferred the rewarded option more after training. But when I changed which option earned the reward, it chose the new option in only three runs, so it failed the full test. This is an engineered prototype, and I haven't established whether its mechanism is biologically sound. The chess part currently records feedback without learning from it.

I define the research question and training rubric, AI makes most of the code, and I am still learning the underlying methods. I have no research adviser. I'd like to develop this into a sound study that I could eventually submit to eLife.

Would you be open to occasional mentorship, starting with whether this question is a useful way to test the approach? I'd appreciate a candid assessment and can send a one-page methods summary first.

Thank you for your time,
Ethan Ramli
High-school student | Jakarta, Indonesia

name: Ronald L. Davis
role: Professor of Neuroscience, University of Florida, Wertheim UF Scripps Institute
need: Reciprocal reward circuitry and active forgetting
title: Reciprocal synapses between mushroom body and dopamine neurons form a positive feedback loop required for learning
finding: Kenyon cells provide cholinergic feedback to dopamine neurons; receptor knockdown impairs learning, and blocking Kenyon-cell output reduces dopamine calcium responses. This constrains a one-way teaching-signal approximation.
second: Associative learning drives longitudinally graded presynaptic plasticity of neurotransmitter release along axonal compartments
https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/76712/elife-76712-v2.pdf
2022 eLife coauthorship with Tomchik: learning modifies acetylcholine release differently across compartments and training valences.
background: His current UF program combines mitochondrial therapeutics with mechanisms of forgetting. Drosophila experiments distinguish permanent active forgetting from transient retrieval failure.
question: Which control separates missing cue-to-dopamine feedback from persistent memory that is temporarily difficult to express?
test: Proposed: measure cue-evoked dopamine activity alongside output and choice; prospectively compare identified reciprocal-pathway perturbation with a matched noninformative-feedback condition. Do not add unsupported omission-driven negative updates.
limit: Reciprocal-feedback evidence does not supply a chess reward mapping or prove all dopamine populations use the same mechanism. Current UF affiliation and address supersede old Scripps-only addresses.
paragraph: Your eLife study of reciprocal Kenyon-cell and dopamine connections made me question my one-way teaching signal. Blocking Kenyon-cell output changed dopamine responses, so feedback seems to depend on the circuit as well as the stimulus supplied to it. Your distinction between active forgetting and temporary retrieval failure also seems relevant to an old choice that persists. What first control would separate a missing feedback interaction from a memory that is stored but expressed incorrectly?
subject: Student mentorship inquiry: reciprocal dopamine feedback and persistent old choices

name: Yi Zhong
role: Professor, School of Life Sciences, Tsinghua University
title: Genetic dissection of mutual interference between two consecutive learning tasks in Drosophila
finding: Proactive and retroactive interference differ in sensitivity to inter-task interval and molecular manipulation. CSW/Raf/MAPK effects on proactive interference are distinguishable from Rac1-related retroactive interference.
second: Differential conditioning produces merged long-term memory in Drosophila
https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/66499/elife-66499-v1.pdf
2021 eLife: single-trial differential conditioning can produce merged avoidance of both experienced cues; spaced experience produces a different memory organization.
background: His Tsinghua group combines fly genetics, behavior, imaging and electrophysiology to study memory and active forgetting. Current faculty records also describe memory-related disease work.
question: Which schedule and probe controls distinguish old-memory interference from a failure to learn the new contingency?
test: Proposed: freeze total cue/reward counts, vary inter-task interval prospectively, and probe both old/new cues plus a novel cue. The completed V1/V2 gates must remain unchanged; further trials use a new specification.
limit: Sequential-task interference and merged aversive memory are not identical to appetitive gamma4 reward reversal. Experimental minutes and molecular manipulations cannot be imported as calibrated software constants.
paragraph: Your eLife work on interference between consecutive learning tasks made me think that my failed reversals may need a better diagnosis than simply more training. The study separates proactive from retroactive interference, and your merged-memory paper shows that the training schedule can change what the animal remembers. What schedule and cue-probe control would you use first to distinguish an old association interfering with the new one from a failure to learn the new contingency?
subject: Student mentorship inquiry: interference or failed updating during reversal

name: Seth M. Tomchik
role: Professor of Neuroscience and Pharmacology and Pediatrics; Roy J. Carver Professor, University of Iowa
need: Compartment-local physiological memory and independent measurements
title: Associative learning drives longitudinally graded presynaptic plasticity of neurotransmitter release along axonal compartments
finding: Acetylcholine-release plasticity is bidirectional and compartment dependent; distinct mechanisms support potentiation and odor contrast. Gamma3 MBONs are implicated in appetitive learning. Calcium, release and downstream choice are separate measurements.
second: Learning and memory program at Iowa
https://neuroscience.grad.uiowa.edu/people/seth-tomchik
Current molecular, cellular and circuit investigations of neuromodulation, sensory acquisition and storage, alongside neurodevelopmental and metabolic research.
background: His current Iowa laboratory combines genetically encoded imaging, optogenetics, behavior and genetics. Older eLife affiliations at Scripps should not be treated as his current institutional address.
question: Which comparison between release and output responses would most decisively falsify a single stored synaptic gain?
test: Proposed: specify independent qualitative predictions for presynaptic release, output activity and choices under appetitive/aversive conditions before changing parameters; initially use a bounded association task and mapped compartments.
limit: The cited behavioral output result concerns gamma3, not the prototype's gamma4 compartment. Measured biological release dynamics do not validate deterministic checkpoint persistence.
paragraph: Your eLife measurements of acetylcholine release made me question what my saved synaptic gain actually represents. Learning changed release in different directions across mushroom-body compartments, and the mechanisms for potentiation and maintaining odor contrast were distinct. My model currently compresses lasting change into one gain on each eligible connection. Which comparison between release and output-neuron responses would most clearly show that this is too simple, before I try to connect it to chess feedback?

name: Leslie C. Griffith
role: Nancy Lurie Marks Professor of Neuroscience; Director, Volen National Center for Complex Systems, Brandeis University
need: Consolidation, physiological state and testable dopamine hypotheses
title: A single pair of neurons links sleep to memory consolidation in Drosophila melanogaster
finding: DPM neurons promote sleep through inhibitory GABA signaling onto wake-promoting mushroom-body neurons. The paper links consolidation-relevant and sleep circuitry; it does not establish that saving state is consolidation.
second: The Role of Dopamine in Associative Learning in Drosophila: An Updated Unified Model
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8192648/
2021 review and proposed integrative model, not new experimental proof: discusses opposing reinforcement components and hypotheses for reward prediction error.
background: Her laboratory links biochemical plasticity, calcium-dependent signaling, experience, sleep and behavior using imaging, electrophysiology and fly genetics.
question: What post-training manipulation would distinguish consolidation from simple persistence of a saved efficacy value?
test: Proposed: distinguish acquisition, post-training processing and later retrieval in a prospective protocol with equal initial performance and matched state/control conditions. A biological consolidation mechanism would require additional evidence before implementation.
limit: DPM sleep circuitry and a review's reward-prediction proposal are distinct evidence levels. The study does not identify the prototype's reward target or establish biological retention.
paragraph: Your eLife study linking sleep and memory consolidation made me reconsider my retention result. My prototype keeps a changed efficacy value because it is saved to disk; that does not show a process that consolidates memory after training. I also read the abstract of your updated dopamine model, which presents testable ideas rather than a ready-made rule. What post-training comparison would you consider essential before a simplified simulation could claim consolidation rather than persistence?
subject: Student mentorship inquiry: consolidation versus saving a changed value

name: Rachel I. Wilson
role: Joseph B. Martin Professor of Basic Research in Neurobiology, Harvard Medical School; HHMI Investigator
need: Physiological assumptions beyond fixed wiring and sensory coding
title: Wiring variations that enable and constrain neural computation in a sensory microcircuit
finding: ORN-to-PN synapse counts covary with dendrite size; lateralized inputs and wiring imprecision affect circuit computation. A connectome count alone is not a calibrated physiological conductance.
second: Current multimodal navigation research
https://www.hhmi.org/scientists/rachel-i-wilson
Electrophysiology, imaging, brain-wide connectomics and models investigate navigation driven by cues, internal drives and remembered information.
background: Her program connects synapses, ion channels and network connectivity to computation in behaving flies. Current work emphasizes navigation and multimodal sensorimotor integration.
question: Which physiological check should come before interpreting graph-preserving cue activity as a plausible sensory representation?
test: Proposed: measure sparsity, excitation/inhibition balance and cue separation under a preregistered input protocol, while keeping wiring fixed and documenting uncertainties in synapse-to-conductance conversion.
limit: Olfactory glomerular physiology is not a validated representation of chess boards or reward reversal. This is an interface/physiology consultation, secondary to fixing biological learning.
paragraph: Your eLife sensory-microcircuit study made me question what preserving a connectome actually guarantees. Synapse number varied together with postsynaptic dendrite size, so treating each anatomical count as a physiological strength could miss compensation. My graph stays fixed, but my input encoding is engineered. Which physiological check would you prioritize before interpreting its cue responses as a defensible sensory representation?
subject: Student mentorship inquiry: what fixed wiring does and does not establish

name: John C. Tuthill
role: Professor, Department of Neurobiology and Biophysics, University of Washington
need: Action readout, feedback and task/circuit separation
title: Central processing of leg proprioception in Drosophila
finding: Identified interneuron types combine position, movement and vibration signals and causally influence posture or pausing. Sensory representation and behavioral output require separate evidence.
second: Current sensorimotor and connectome-simulation program
https://faculty.washington.edu/tuthill/research.html
The lab studies feedback-guided movement and reports connectome simulations of a walking central pattern generator; this is a research-program reference, not full review of that separate paper.
background: His laboratory combines cell-type targeting, electrophysiology, imaging and behavioral measurements to study proprioception and motor control, with computational collaborations.
question: Which readout ablation distinguishes a choice produced by the simulated circuit from one imposed by the software decoder?
test: Proposed: report unaided circuit-driven choices under a frozen decoder, compare decoder-only and neural-state perturbation controls, and measure sensitivity to the simulated state independently of external chess search.
limit: A chess move is not a leg motor command. Proprioceptive feedback differs from reinforcement feedback, and the brain-only graph cannot silently be treated as a complete embodied walking circuit.
paragraph: Your eLife proprioception study connects to a boundary I want to make clearer in my project. You identify sensory-response types and then test how activating them changes posture or pausing. I currently turn output activity into a discrete choice through a software decoder, and I worry that this decoder could account for too much of the behavior. What readout control would distinguish a decision produced by the simulated circuit from a choice imposed by the interface?

name: Christopher J. Potter
role: Professor of Neuroscience, Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine
need: Verified sensory neuron identities and functional annotation
title: Chemoreceptor co-expression in Drosophila melanogaster olfactory neurons
finding: Genetic knock-ins and recordings reveal extensive olfactory co-receptor co-expression, challenging a simple one-family-per-neuron assumption. Labels require functional checks.
second: Food odors trigger Drosophila males to deposit a pheromone that guides aggregation and female oviposition decisions
https://elifesciences.org/articles/08688
2015 eLife: receptor/cell manipulations connect Or7a-mediated sensory detection to aggregation and egg-laying behavior.
background: His current official research emphasis is Anopheles mosquito olfaction, with earlier Drosophila sensory-circuit work and genetic tools. Fly-specific expertise remains relevant but current program mismatch is explicit.
question: What minimal functional evidence should accompany an annotation-based assignment of synthetic cues to sensory neurons?
test: Proposed: document actual released-graph annotations, distinguish anatomical identity from receptor expression/function, and validate cue selectivity against independent evidence before assigning a sensory interface.
limit: His current emphasis is mosquitoes and sensory entry rather than gamma4 reversal. Receptor identities do not justify arbitrary chess-feature-to-neuron mappings.
paragraph: Your eLife co-receptor study made me cautious about choosing sensory inputs from labels alone. The overlap between receptor families was broader than the usual simple classification suggests, and you checked function as well as expression. My chess input would be an engineered stimulus, so I need to state that boundary honestly. What minimum functional evidence should accompany an annotation-based choice of input neurons? I realize your current focus is mosquito olfaction, so a brief pointer would also be helpful.
subject: Student mentorship inquiry: evidence for a defensible sensory input mapping
